q: how many ml of Tylenol for a 22 pound baby
text:
22 lb = 10 kg.

• Dose: 150 mg every 4–6 h (max 4 doses/day).
  – Tylenol Children's / Infants', syrup 160 mg/5 ml: 4.6 ml

q: can I give Motrin to my 8 month old for fever
text:
Yes, ibuprofen (Motrin) can be given to children over 6 months old, according to MedlinePlus [6]. Give it every 6 to 8 hours, and know your child's weight before giving it [6]. The SEUP adds that the dose is the one your paediatrician recommends, and that the goal is your child's comfort rather than bringing the fever down on its own [2].

Do not give ibuprofen if your child is dehydrated, has chickenpox, or has asthma unless a doctor has said it is OK [3]. Do not alternate ibuprofen and paracetamol unless a doctor or nurse tells you to [3].

Get medical advice if:
- Your child is not their usual self or is not interested in feeding [3]
- They show signs of dehydration, such as nappies that are not very wet, sunken eyes, or no tears when crying [3]
- The fever lasts 5 days or more [3]
- You are worried, or the medicine is not helping [4]

q: my son threw up twice this morning, what should I give him to drink
text:
Vomiting twice in a morning is often gastroenteritis, which is usually not serious in healthy people but can sometimes lead to dehydration, according to MedlinePlus [2].

What to do now: the priority is to keep fluids going in. Wait 20 minutes after a vomit, then give oral rehydration solution, 2–5 ml every 5 minutes for an hour, says the SEUP [3]. If he keeps it down, you can slowly increase how often you offer it [3]. Don't use homemade solutions like lemonade or commercial soft drinks [3]. Keep offering his normal food in smaller, more frequent amounts; no need to fast, and dairy and breastfeeding are fine [4]. Sports drinks should be avoided [4].

Get help if:
- He vomits a lot, can't keep down solids or liquids, or vomits even without drinking [7]
- Vomit is green, bloody, or looks like coffee grounds [7]
- He is drowsy, limp, very thirsty, has sunken eyes, cries without tears, or urinates little [7]
- Severe belly pain or headache [7]
- Under 3 months old and has vomited two or more feeds [7]

q: how do I know if my child is getting dehydrated from vomiting
text:
The biggest risk from vomiting is dehydration, which happens when a child loses more fluid than they take in [1][3].

What to do now: give an oral rehydration solution. After your child vomits, wait 20 minutes, then give 2–5 ml every 5 minutes for an hour, according to the SEUP [4]. If they keep it down, you can slowly offer it more often [4]. Don't use homemade drinks like lemonade or commercial soft drinks [4]. Keep breastfeeding normally, and offer small, frequent meals — no need to fast [5].

Signs to watch for and get help:
- Drowsy, limp or very thirsty [7]
- Sunken eyes, crying without tears, or passing little urine [7]
- Vomiting a lot, can't keep down solids or liquids, or vomits even without drinking [7]
- Green vomit, blood, or brown coffee-ground material [7]
- Under 3 months old and vomited two or more feeds [7]

q: my 5 year old has been coughing all night, what can I do
text:
A cough that keeps a child awake at night is common with colds and flu, and both usually get better on their own [3][5]. For a 5-year-old, the things that help are simple: offer plenty of fluids, let them rest, and run a clean humidifier or cool-mist vaporizer in the room [3]. Saline nose drops or spray can also ease a blocked nose [3].

Be careful with cough and cold medicines: some contain ingredients not recommended for children, so talk to your child's doctor before giving any [3]. Never give aspirin to a child [3].

Get medical help if your child has:
- Trouble breathing or fast breathing [3]
- Signs of dehydration [3]
- Fever lasting more than 4 days [3]
- Symptoms lasting more than 10 days with no improvement [3]
- Symptoms that improve, then come back or get worse [3]

Coughing that is worse at night can also be a sign of asthma in children [4].

q: my son has been coughing for a week after a cold
text:
A cough lasting about a week after a cold is common, and cold symptoms can last 10 to 14 days [6]. In whooping cough, the first signs are also cold-like — runny nose, mild fever, mild occasional cough — and last 1 to 2 weeks before the cough gets worse [3].

What to do now: keep offering fluids, and keep the room free of smoke and fumes, which can trigger coughing [1]. There is no home treatment in these sources that shortens a cough; if you are worried, your doctor can assess your son.

Get medical care if:
- Coughing fits that are worse at night, or a high-pitched "whoop" between coughs [3][4]
- Vomiting during or after coughing fits [3]
- Difficulty breathing after a coughing bout, or turning blue or grey [4]
- A pause in breathing (apnea) in a baby [3]
- Cough getting worse instead of better after a week [3][4]

q: he has a cough but no fever and is eating normally
text:
A cough without fever, with normal eating, is usually a mild illness — fever is the body's natural response to fighting infections like coughs and colds, according to the NHS [1]. Keep offering fluids and normal meals; a poor diet for a few days won't hurt [3].

Watch for these signs and get help if they appear:
- Fever of 38°C (100.4 °F) or higher in a baby under 3 months [1]
- Fever lasting 5 days or more [1]
- Not wanting to eat, or not their usual self [1]
- Dehydration — fewer wet nappies, sunken eyes, no tears [1]
- Difficulty breathing, or skin/lips turning blue or grey [1]

q: my daughter has red spots all over her stomach and they appeared today
text:
Red spots that appear suddenly should be checked by a doctor, since the information available does not describe what causes them or how they usually progress.

While you arrange that, keep your daughter comfortable and let her keep her normal activity if she is otherwise well [4]. Offer fluids and watch her nappies or toilet visits so you know when she last passed urine and how her stools look [4].

Get medical help if she has any of these:
- Looks unwell, floppy, pale, or refuses food [6]
- Stomach pain that is continuous or getting worse, or that wakes her at night [2]
- Pain on the right side of the abdomen [2]
- Repeated vomiting that is green, brown or bloody [2]
- Black, tar-like stools or blood in the stool [2]
- A tense, hard or swollen abdomen [2]

q: my 2 year old has little red bumps on his legs and keeps scratching them
text:
Itchy red bumps on the legs are common in small children, and one cause is eczema, which most often causes dry, itchy skin and rashes, according to MedlinePlus [2]. Scratching can make the skin red, swollen and itch even more [2]. Eczema is not contagious [2].

What helps: keep the skin well cared for and avoid things that irritate it, such as certain soaps, fabrics and lotions, stress, and things your child is allergic to like foods, pollen and animals [2]. Treatments may include medicines, skin creams and light therapy [2].

See your doctor if:
- The rash spreads or gets worse [2]
- The skin becomes very red, swollen or itchy despite care [2]
- Your child seems unwell or the itching disturbs sleep [2]

q: these spots dont seem to bother her but there are more every morning
text:
Spots that spread or increase over days can have several causes, and the pattern matters more than the spots themselves. Scabies causes intensely itchy bumps and lines, worse at night, on fingers, wrists, arms, legs and around the waist, according to the WHO [1]. Eczema causes dry, itchy skin with a rash on the face, inside the elbows, behind the knees, hands and feet, and it is not contagious, according to MedlinePlus [2]. Measles rash starts as flat red spots at the hairline and spreads downward, usually with fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes, according to the CDC [5].

See your doctor if:
- The spots keep spreading or multiplying each day [1][5]
- She develops fever, cough, runny nose or red eyes [5][6]
- The skin becomes raw, scaly, or she seems uncomfortable or distressed [3][4]
- The spots become crusty, weepy or look infected [1]

A doctor can look at the rash and tell you what it is and how to treat it.

q: my 6 year old fell from the bed and hit the back of his head
text:
Most head injuries in children are not serious, and most children recover quickly [2][6]. For the next 24 hours, watch him closely for any sign that something is wrong [3].

What you can do now: he can sleep, but after a more significant knock it is worth waking him every 4 hours [6]. He can eat and drink as usual, according to his appetite [6]. If he has a headache, you can give ibuprofen or paracetamol at the dose your doctor indicates [6]. Keep him resting from sport and screens for 24 to 48 hours, then return to normal activities gradually [4].

Get medical help now if he:
- has been knocked out or cannot stay awake [2]
- has a seizure, or new weakness or numbness [2]
- is vomiting repeatedly [4]
- is confused, or hard to wake [4]
- has clear fluid or blood from the nose or ears [4]
- has trouble walking, speaking or balancing [2]

q: what foods should I start with for a baby who just turned 6 months
text:
Around 6 months, breast milk or formula alone no longer meets all your baby's energy and nutrient needs, so solid foods should start now, according to the WHO [1]. At first, how much they eat matters less than getting used to eating; they still get most energy and nutrients from milk [2].

Start with small amounts and increase gradually as your baby grows, and build up the consistency and variety of foods over time [1]. Offer 2–3 meals a day at this age [1]. Introduce one food at a time so you can spot any allergic reaction, such as a rash, diarrhoea or vomiting [5].

Keep giving breast milk or formula alongside the solids [2].

Avoid these:
- Honey before age 1 (risk of botulism) [5]
- Cow's milk before age 1 [5]
- Unpasteurised drinks or foods [5]
- Choking hazards: sweets, popcorn, whole nuts, whole grapes [5]

Ask your baby's doctor when to start and about peanut-containing foods if there is eczema or egg allergy [5].

q: how much water can a 9 month old drink
text:
For a 9-month-old, breast milk or formula stays the main drink, and water is not needed in large amounts. The AEP says that between 6 and 12 months breast milk remains the main food and should be kept on demand, without reducing the number of feeds [2]. If a baby over 6 months has at least 4–5 breastfeeds a day, no other milk source is needed [2].

What to do now: keep offering breast milk or formula on demand, and give water only in small amounts with meals, from a cup. During an illness, the WHO says to increase fluid intake, including how often you breastfeed, and to offer soft, favourite foods [1].

When to get help:
- Fewer wet nappies, sunken eyes, or a dry mouth [1]
- Refusing all feeds or drinks [1]
- Vomiting or diarrhoea that will not stop [1]
- Sleepy, floppy, or hard to wake [1]
- Fever in a baby this age [1]

q: my baby refuses vegetables but eats fruit all day
text: It is common for babies to prefer fruit, and the way to build liking for vegetables is repeated, varied exposure rather than pressure. The AEP advises introducing the whole variety of fruits and vegetables gradually, at any daily meal, and varying how they are offered — puréed, mashed or in small pieces [1]. Taste for different flavours, including bitter ones like some vegetables, is formed early, and early exposure to different flavours may reduce the risk of refusing new foods [1]. Offer vegetables alongside fruit at meals, and keep offering them even if refused; the NHS suggests including vegetables with bitter flavours such as broccoli, cauliflower, spinach and cabbage [3]. Give whole fruit rather than juice, since juice offers no nutritional benefit over whole fruit and can displace other foods [1]. For green leafy vegetables like spinach or chard in the first year, keep them under 20% of the dish because of nitrates [1].

q: my daughter is 13 months and still mostly drinks formula
text:
At 13 months, formula alone no longer meets a child's energy and nutrient needs: around 6 months those needs start to exceed what milk provides, and complementary foods are needed to cover them [2]. The WHO guiding principles are to keep breastfeeding (or formula) on demand up to 2 years or more, while giving solid foods from 6 months [2][3].

What to do now: offer 3–4 meals a day plus 1–2 snacks as needed, starting with small amounts and gradually increasing quantity, consistency and variety [2]. Feed to appetite, following hunger and fullness cues, and keep good hygiene when handling food [2].

See your doctor if you are worried about her growth or eating — the AEP notes that if complementary foods are not introduced around 6 months, or are given too early, growth can be affected [2].

q: how often should a newborn poop
text:
How often a newborn poops varies from baby to baby — the rhythm and consistency of stools differs from one person to another, according to the SEUP [3]. It is not essential that a baby has a bowel movement every day [3].

For a baby under 6 months, keep feeding as usual with breast milk or formula [3]. Your baby's doctor will want to keep an eye on constipation unless it comes with any of these signs [3]:

- Important belly pain, or a baby who is very down and complaining a lot [3]
- Blood in the stool [3]
- Vomiting many times, not keeping down solids or liquids [3]
- Pain when passing stool [3]

Call your doctor if you notice any of these.

q: my 9 month old suddenly wakes up every two hours at night
text:
Waking every two hours at night is common at this age: night wakings are physiological, and around 30% of children still wake at night by one year, according to PUC Chile [1]. The usual cause in healthy babies is habit — how they fall asleep — rather than illness [6].

What helps: put your baby down still awake, so they learn to fall asleep on their own; if they always fall asleep in your arms, they will look for that same condition when they wake [1]. If they wake, give them the chance to settle back by themselves before going in [1]. Sleep cycles last about 90 minutes [1].

See your doctor if:
- Waking comes with fever, poor feeding or unusual irritability [6]
- Symptoms of reflux, cow's milk allergy or ear infection [6]
- You feel the waking is affecting your baby's or the family's wellbeing [6]

q: my 4 year old wakes up coughing only when he lies down
text:
A cough that comes on at night or early in the morning is one of the symptoms of asthma in children, according to MedlinePlus [5]. In preschoolers, the most common trigger of this kind of cough and wheeze is a viral respiratory infection, according to the SEUP [1].

What to do now: keep giving fluids and keep the room free of tobacco smoke, since children of smokers get more respiratory illnesses [7]. If your child has been prescribed a bronchodilator such as salbutamol, it must be given with a spacer, never straight into the mouth, because it works less well that way [7]. - Severe coughing or serious trouble breathing [5]

q: she is making a strange noise when she breathes but is still smiling
text:
A strange noise when breathing can be a sign of croup, an inflammation of the voice box and windpipe that often starts like a cold and causes noisy, sharp sounds when breathing in, according to MedlinePlus [3]. It is usually caused by a virus and most viral cases are mild and can be treated at home [3]. Symptoms often get worse at night and last three to five days [3].

Keep your child calm and comfortable, and offer fluids often. Croup often starts as a cold, so watch how she breathes over the next few days [3].

Get help if:
- Breathing becomes difficult or she is breathing fast [1][4]
- The ribs pull in or the chest sinks with each breath [1][2][4]
- She seems drowsy, very irritable or generally unwell [1][4]
- She refuses to eat or drink [4]
- You are worried about her breathing [3]

q: my 6 year old says his chest hurts when he takes a deep breath

Chest pain when breathing deeply can have several causes, and one of them is asthma: chest tightness that makes it hard to breathe deeply is a common symptom, according to the WHO [2]. Symptoms like these should be discussed with a healthcare provider [2].

If your child has a cold or a cough along with it, watch for these signs at home: breathing that is fast, ribs pulling in, or the chest sinking in, and chest pain when breathing [1]. Also watch for tiredness when walking or running [1].

- He seems generally unwell, drowsy, or very irritable [1][5]

- He refuses food and fluids [5]

q: my daughter is crying nonstop after a fall and wont calm down

A fall on the head can cause headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and drowsiness, and most head injuries in children are mild [1]. - A headache that gets worse or does not go away [4]

- Being very irritable or hard to wake, or any behaviour that worries you [6][5]

q: my baby had a seizure last year and has a fever today
text:
A febrile seizure can happen when a child has a high temperature, and it is not usually serious, according to the NHS [3]. Most febrile seizures do not need treatment, but a child needs to be checked in hospital after a first febrile seizure [6].

If your child has another seizure now: do not move them or hold them in place, do not put anything in their mouth, and do not try to lower their temperature by undressing them or sponging them with cold water [5].

Get help if your child:
- has a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes [2]
- has difficulty breathing [2]
- has stiffness and twitching on only one side [2]
- is more sleepy than usual for over 1 hour after it stops [2]
- has more than one seizure within 24 hours [2]

You cannot prevent febrile seizures [6].

q: my child has a sore throat and white stuff on the tonsils
text:
A sore throat with white patches on the tonsils is often tonsillitis, an infection of the tonsils that is a common childhood illness, according to the NHS [1]. The white patches can come with a sore throat, trouble swallowing, a high temperature, coughing, a headache, feeling sick, earache and tiredness [1].

To help at home: offer plenty of water, cool or soft foods, and rest; avoid smoky places [6]. Ice cubes, ice lollies or hard sweets can soothe the throat, but do not give young children anything small and hard to suck because of the risk of choking [6]. Do not have your child gargle warm salty water — children should not try this [6].

Get medical help if:
- White pus-filled spots on the tonsils [2]
- A sore throat so painful it is hard to eat or drink [2]
- Symptoms not gone within 1 week [2]
- A severe sore throat that quickly gets worse, swelling inside the mouth or throat, trouble speaking, swallowing, breathing or opening the mouth [3]

q: my 3 year old was stung by a bee on the hand
text:
A bee sting on the hand is a common injury, and most children recover fully. The main concern is a severe allergic reaction called anaphylaxis, which can start within minutes of the sting and affects several organs at once [4].

Watch your child closely for the first while. If a severe reaction is happening and an adrenaline auto-injector is available, it should be used straight away, injected into the outer thigh [1][4].

- Swelling of the eyelids, lips or ears [4]
- Trouble breathing, cough or wheezing [4]
- Dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness [4]
- Vomiting [4]

If none of these appear, keep the hand clean and comfortable and watch for any swelling that spreads.

q: my baby has a temperature of 100.4, is that considered a fever
text:
100.4 °F = 38 °C.

If your baby is under 3 months old, a fever needs a doctor the same day. For an older baby, a temperature of 100.4 °F (38 °C (100.4 °F)) is considered a fever, according to the NHS [3].

Fever is not a disease — it is usually a sign the body is fighting an infection, and most fevers in children are caused by common illnesses like coughs and colds [5][6]. You can usually look after them at home, and the temperature should come down over 1 to 4 days [2].

What to do now:
- Offer plenty of fluids; if breastfeeding, keep feeding as normal [2].
- Check on them regularly, including during the night [2].
- Keep them at home, and don't sponge them down or wrap them in too many clothes [2][5].
- If they are distressed or uncomfortable, you can give paracetamol or ibuprofen — check the leaflet for your child's age, and ask a pharmacist or doctor if unsure. The dose depends on their age and weight [2].

Get medical advice if:
- They are under 3 months and have a temperature of 38 °C (100.4 °F) or higher [5].
- They are 3 to 6 months and have a temperature of 39 °C (102.2 °F) or higher [5].
- They have a rash along with the fever [5].
- The fever has lasted 5 days or more [5].
- They are not feeding, not themselves, or show signs of dehydration [5].

q: can I put aloe on my baby's sunburn
text:
No, do not put petroleum jelly on sunburnt skin, and do not put ice or ice packs on it either, according to the NHS [3]. Also do not pop any blisters, do not scratch or try to remove peeling skin, and do not wear tight-fitting clothes over the sunburnt skin [3].

For a baby with sunburn, keep them out of the sun and offer fluids often. If they have been in high heat and are not well, take them to a cool place, remove extra clothing, use cool wet cloths and fans to help them lose heat, and give them water in small sips, according to the SEUP [1][2].

Get help if:
- Fever above 39°C (102.2 °F) that does not come down with home measures [6]
- Loss of consciousness or seizures [6]
- Confusion, trouble speaking or moving [6]
- Persistent vomiting and unable to drink [6]

q: my newborn is not waking up to feed as much as before
text:

q: how many wet diapers should a 4 month old have
text:
A 4-month-old should be wetting diapers frequently, with clear, odourless urine — especially if they are breastfed only [4]. There is no single exact number the guidance gives; what matters is that wetting continues often and the urine stays clear.

Watch for these signs of dehydration, according to MedlinePlus:
- No wet diaper for 3 hours or more [1][3]
- Dry mouth and tongue [1]
- Crying without tears [1]
- Unusual sleepiness or irritability [1]
- Sunken eyes [1]

Get medical help right away if there is confusion, fainting, no urination, fast heartbeat or fast breathing [1]. For babies, any fever, or diarrhoea lasting more than a day, also means seeing a health professional as soon as possible [3].

q: can babies get dehydrated from breastfeeding
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, little urine, dry mouth, persistent vomiting or heavy diarrhoea >24 h
text:
Yes, babies can get dehydrated, and breastfeeding is one of the best protections against it. Dehydration happens when the body loses more fluid than it takes in [2]. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months is a key way to prevent it, and breast milk should be continued — even more often if the baby wants it — during diarrhoea or vomiting [4][1].

What to do now: keep breastfeeding normally, and offer the breast more frequently if your baby demands it [1]. If your baby is also vomiting, wait 20 minutes after a vomit, then give oral rehydration solution, 2–5 ml every 5 minutes for an hour, and increase the frequency slowly if it is well tolerated [5]. Do not use homemade solutions or commercial soft drinks [5].

Get help if:
- Sunken eyes, little urine, dry mouth [4]
- Persistent vomiting or vomiting even without taking anything [1]
- Vomits green, bloody or coffee-ground material [1]
- Blood in the stools or diarrhoea that keeps going [4]

q: should I give my daughter the HPV vaccine
text:
The HPV vaccine protects against human papillomavirus, a common virus spread through skin contact, usually during sex; some types are linked to cervical, mouth, anal, penile, vulval and vaginal cancer, and to genital warts [2]. It works very well: since it has been used there has been a big drop in young people getting conditions linked to HPV, such as cervical cancer and genital warts [4]. In the United States it is given as part of the national childhood schedule; the ages follow the United States national schedule [2].

After the injection, the most common side effects are mild and do not last long: swelling or pain where the injection was given, headache, a high temperature, dizziness, feeling sick, tiredness [5].

Get help if:
- swelling or pain at the injection site [5]
- headache or high temperature [5]
- dizziness, feeling sick or tiredness [5]
- a severe allergic reaction — very rare; the person who vaccinates is trained to treat it immediately [5]

q: my son missed his 4 month vaccines, what do we do now
text:
A missed vaccine dose does not mean starting over: the child should receive the same schedule as other babies, with the same timing, according to the AEP [2]. The unit dose of each vaccine is the same as for any other baby, and there is no basis for reduced or split doses [1].

What to do now: book an appointment with your doctor or clinic to catch up. Between doses of the same vaccine there should be an interval of 4 weeks to 6 months depending on the vaccine, though the minimum is usually around 8 weeks [6]. The ages in the schedule follow the United States national schedule.

Get help or advice if:
- Your child is unwell with a fever or infection — vaccination may need to be temporarily postponed [1].
- Your child was born very prematurely (≤28 weeks) — they may need breathing monitoring for 48–72 hours after vaccination [3].
- You are unsure which doses are due — your doctor can check the record [2].

q: I gave my son Tylenol and he vomited 10 minutes later
text:
A single vomit after a dose of medicine is common and usually not a reason to worry. Vomiting is often caused by a stomach bug and usually stops in a few days [5].

Keep giving fluids: offer water in small sips if he feels sick, and if he is on formula or solid foods, give small sips of water between feeds [5]. Let him eat when he is able, avoiding fatty or spicy foods [5]. If he vomits again, do not repeat the paracetamol dose — wait and check with your doctor or pharmacist about when the next dose is due.

Get help if:
- He is under 3 months and has vomited two or more feeds [2]
- He vomits a lot, cannot keep down solids or liquids, or vomits even without taking anything [2]
- The vomit is green, contains blood, or looks like coffee grounds [2]

q: my toddler has a swollen eyelid after waking up
text:
A swollen eyelid in a toddler can be one of the early signs of roseola, a very common infection in babies and toddlers, according to the NHS [3]. In roseola, swollen eyelids and swollen neck glands appear at first, along with a sudden high temperature and cold-like symptoms such as a sore throat, runny nose and cough; these last 3 to 5 days, before a rash appears [3].

Swelling of the eyelids can also be part of a severe allergic reaction, so it is worth knowing the signs that mean it is more serious, according to the SEUP [6]:

- Trouble breathing or noisy breathing [5]
- Drooling or bluish lips [5]
- Paleness [5]
- Loss of consciousness [5]
- Swelling of the eyelids, lips or ears with itching, widespread redness, hives, dizziness or vomiting [6]

If any of these appear, use any prescribed adrenaline auto-injector straight away and get medical help immediately [5].

- Drowsy and hard to wake, or extremely agitated [2]
- Difficulty breathing, grunting, or breathing very fast [2]

- A rash appears with the fever [7]
- A rash does not fade when you roll a glass over it [7]
- You are worried, or the medicine is not helping [3]

- seems generally unwell, irritable, or is not feeding, eating or drinking properly [6]
- is sick (vomiting) [6]

Red cheeks alone do not mean your baby has a fever. q: my son is 4 and weighs 25 pounds, is that too little
text:
25 lb = 11.3 kg.

I can't tell you whether 25 pounds is too little for your son from what I have here. What the sources do say is how growth is judged: weight alone isn't the measure — it's weight for height (or BMI for height) plotted on a growth chart, and the position on that curve over time is what matters [4]. The WHO growth standards are the reference used for this, and they let health workers spot underweight or overweight early [2]. A single weight, without his height and his curve, doesn't settle it.

What to do: ask your doctor to plot his weight and height on the WHO chart for his age and sex and show you where he sits [4]. A change in his growth curve is the signal to look closer, and the measurement should be rechecked first to be sure it was taken correctly [4].

Warning signs to mention to your doctor:
- Weight falling across curve lines [4]
- Poor weight gain or weight loss [7]

q: what should I know about malaria symptoms in a child returning from Africa
text:
Malaria is a potentially fatal disease spread by mosquito bites, and the first symptoms are often mild and hard to recognise as malaria [1]. The most common early symptoms are fever, headache and chills, usually appearing 10 to 15 days after an infected mosquito bite [2]. Because these symptoms are not specific, a test should be done as soon as possible [2]. Early treatment of a mild case can stop the infection getting worse [2].

Get medical help urgently if your child has:

- Extreme tiredness and fatigue [2]
- Deteriorating consciousness [2]
- Seizures [2]
- Difficulty breathing [2]
- Dark or bloody urine, yellowing of eyes and skin, or abnormal bleeding [2]

Infants, children under 5, pregnant women, travellers and people with HIV or AIDS are at greater risk of severe infection [2].

q: my child coughs mostly at night but is fine during the day
text:
A cough that is worse at night and fine during the day is common in several childhood conditions, and the pattern alone does not tell them apart. Croup causes a dry, barking cough and hoarse voice, and the symptoms usually get worse at night and last three to five days, according to MedlinePlus [6]. Asthma can also cause cough, and it may be hard to diagnose in young children because the symptoms look like other childhood illnesses [3].

If the cough comes with a cold, keep the child comfortable and offer fluids. Croup is often caused by a virus and most viral cases are mild and can be treated at home [6].

See a doctor if:
- Breathing gets harder, faster, or you see the ribs pulling in [7]
- The child is very agitated or sleepy, or turns blue or pale [7]
- A barking cough comes with noisy breathing or trouble breathing [6]
- Coughing fits are followed by a whoop, vomiting, or exhaustion [2]

q: my son has had a dry cough for three weeks
text:
A dry cough lasting three weeks or more is a reason to have your child examined for tuberculosis, according to the Ministério da Saúde [1]. In babies under 1 year, and especially under 6 months, whooping cough is also a concern: it can start as a mild dry cough and become severe, with coughing fits, trouble breathing, vomiting and dehydration, and these babies need hospital care [6].

Because your baby is under 3 months old, do not give any cough or cold medicine at home — talk to your child's health professional before giving any medicine [5].

See a doctor now if your baby has:
- Trouble breathing or fast breathing [5]
- Coughing fits, or turning red or bluish in the face [6]
- Vomiting or signs of dehydration [6]
- Fever lasting more than 4 days [5]
- Symptoms lasting more than 10 days without getting better [5]

q: my daughter has a wet cough but no fever
text:
A wet cough without a fever is usually caused by a common infection like a cough or cold, according to the NHS [1]. A high temperature is the body's natural response to fighting infections like coughs and colds [1].

Keep your child comfortable and offer plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration [2]. If they seem uncomfortable, acetaminophen or ibuprofen can help; the dose depends on your child's weight [2]. Do not give aspirin to a child with a fever [2].

See a doctor if your child:
- is not their usual self and you're worried [1]
- does not want to eat [1]
- is dehydrated — diapers that are not very wet, sunken eyes, no tears when crying [1]
- has a cough along with night sweats that wake them or worry you [3]
- has difficulty breathing, breathlessness or breathing very fast [1]

A cough after choking can be a sign that something is still in the airway, so it needs checking. The NHS says to get help if a child is struggling to breathe, choking, gasping or unable to speak [3].

- Their skin, lips or tongue turn pale, blue or blotchy [3]
- They cough up blood [3]

text:
A baby who was choking and is breathing normally now still needs to be checked, because the airways can swell or something can stay lodged after the first episode. While you get help, keep your baby upright and calm, and do not put anything in their mouth or give food or drink, according to the SEUP [4].

- Breathing fast, ribs pulling in, or chest sinking [4]
- Chest or side pain when breathing [4]
- Pale, bluish or grey colour [4]
- Floppy, sleepy or very irritable [4]
- Refusing feeds and fluids [4]

Get help now if you see:

- Breathing much faster than usual [2][3]
- Blue or pale colour [3]

- Refusing all food and fluids [3]

q: my daughter fainted for a few seconds at school and feels fine now
text:
A short faint like this is called a syncope: a sudden, brief loss of consciousness that usually happens when not enough blood or oxygen reaches the brain, according to the SEUP [2]. It often follows heat, pain, fear, anxiety, standing still for a long time, or getting up too quickly [2].

What helps now: if she feels unwell again, have her sit or lie down right away, and breathe slowly and deeply [5]. If she faints, lay her with her legs raised and her head to one side [5]. After resting, children usually recover within a couple of minutes, and she can sit up slowly, then stand after a few minutes [5].

Get medical help if:
- She takes more than 3-5 minutes to come round [6]
- It happened during exercise or while sitting [6]
- There were palpitations, chest pain, jerking, or she wet herself [6]

q: my teenager fainted during soccer practice
text:
Fainting (syncope) is a sudden, short loss of consciousness that happens when not enough blood or oxygen reaches the brain, according to the SEUP [2]. It can be brought on by heat, standing still for a long time, or getting up quickly [2].

If your teenager feels faint again, have them sit or lie down right away and breathe slowly and deeply [5]. If they lose consciousness, lay them on their side with their legs raised [5]. They usually recover within a couple of minutes of rest [5]. Encourage them to drink more fluids, especially during exercise [4].

Get medical help now if they:
- fainted while exercising [3][6]
- are not breathing, or cannot be woken within 1 minute [3]
- have not fully recovered, or have trouble speaking or moving [3]
- have chest pain or a pounding or irregular heartbeat [3][6]
- are shaking or jerking [3]

Blurred vision after a blow to the face needs to be checked, because a head injury can affect the eyes and vision [5]. While you get your child seen, keep them still and do not let them rub the eye or the face [5].

- Headache that gets worse or does not go away [5]
- Repeated vomiting or nausea [5]
- Dilated pupil in one or both eyes [5]
- Trouble speaking, weakness or numbness in arms or legs [5]
- Growing confusion, or hard to wake up [5]

After a head injury, rest from physical and mental activity for 24 to 48 hours is recommended, with no sports or screens, according to the SEUP [6].

text:
Vomiting with a stomach bug usually settles in a few days, and the main aim now is to keep fluids going in [3]. Give small sips of water or an oral rehydration solution often, and keep breastfeeding or formula feeding — if they are sick, offer smaller feeds more often than usual [2][3]. - Vomiting a lot, not keeping down solids or liquids, or vomiting even without eating [6]
- Vomit is green, bloody, or looks like coffee grounds [6]
- Drowsy, floppy, very thirsty, sunken eyes, crying without tears, or passing little urine [6]
- Severe tummy pain or headache [6]

A child who turns blue around the lips needs help right away — that is a sign of a severe attack, according to MedlinePlus [2]. While you get help, keep your child upright or semi-seated and stay with them [6]. Do not give anything by mouth if they are struggling to breathe [3].

q: mi niño tiene asma y le cuesta un poquito respirar
banner: 🚨 Llama ahora al 911 o acude a urgencias. | Motivo: Dificultad para respirar grave (se marcan las costillas, respira muy rápido, pausas en la respiración, color azulado)
text:
Las crisis asmáticas son episodios de tos, dificultad para respirar y ruidos de pecho producidos por obstrucción de los bronquios, según la SEUP [2]. En casa, administra de 2 a 4 pulsaciones de salbutamol, de una en una, con cámara espaciadora (y mascarilla facial en niños pequeños), y repite esa dosis a los 10-15 minutos [6]. Mantenlo en reposo, sin ejercicio, y evita el humo del tabaco o la contaminación [6]. Si toma tratamiento de mantenimiento, debe seguir con él durante la crisis [6]. Si la crisis no cede tras el tratamiento en casa, o si te queda alguna duda, acude lo antes posible a un centro sanitario y lleva la cámara espaciadora [6].

Vigila estos signos:
- Respiración cada vez más rápida [7].
- Labios morados o palidez [7].
- Cada vez más decaído, menos activo, con dificultad para hablar o comer [7].
- Necesita inhalaciones cada dos horas o menos [3].
- Se le marcan las costillas, mueve mucho el abdomen o se le hunde el pecho [3].

q: my 18 month old has a fever of 103 and won't take Tylenol

103 °F = 39.4 °C.

A fever is usually a sign the body is fighting an infection, and most children get better within 1 to 4 days, according to the NHS [5]. The goal at home is your child's comfort, not bringing the number down by itself [3].

Keep offering plenty of fluids in small amounts, dress them lightly and don't overbundle them, and don't force food if they don't want it [3]. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) and ibuprofen both reduce fever; acetaminophen can be given every 4 to 6 hours and ibuprofen every 6 to 8 hours, and you need to know your child's weight before giving either [4]. If they refuse the medicine, keep them hydrated and comfortable and try again later [3].

Get help if:
- Fever lasts more than 4 days [5]
- A seizure or fit happens [5]
- They seem very unwell, floppy or hard to wake [5]
- They are drinking much less or have fewer wet diapers [3]

q: can I give him both Tylenol and Motrin at the same time
text:
No, do not give ibuprofen and paracetamol at the same time, according to the NHS [2]. You can alternate between them only if a doctor or nurse tells you to; if they do, write down when you gave each medicine so the doses are spaced evenly and you do not give too much [2].

If one is not helping your child's symptoms, you can try the other instead, as long as it is suitable for your child [2]. Ibuprofen can be given 3 to 4 times in 24 hours, depending on your child's age and dose — check the packet or leaflet [2]. Acetaminophen is given every 4 to 6 hours and ibuprofen every 6 to 8 hours [1].

q: why does my 3 year old have a temperature of 105 degree celsius
text:
105 °F = 40.6 °C.

A temperature of 105 °C is not possible — a thermometer reading that high means the measurement is wrong, so check it again. Fever itself is not an illness: it is a sign the body is fighting an infection, and most fevers are caused by infections [1]. Fever is very common in young children [3].

If your child does have a fever, take the temperature with a digital thermometer, in the armpit or rectally, which is most accurate [5]. Before treating it, look at how your child is: if there are no warning signs, start with physical measures — remove extra clothing, give fluids, reduce activity, and a lukewarm bath if your child is comfortable [5]. Fever rarely goes above 40.5 °C (104.9 °F) on its own [5].

Get medical help if your child is very sleepy, confused, irritable or behaving abnormally, or has a severe headache or repeated vomiting [6].

q: how long does flu last in toddlers
text:
Most children get better from flu on their own, and in most cases the fever and other symptoms go away within a week without needing medical care, according to the WHO [5]. The cough can be intense and last two weeks or more [5].

While your child is ill: keep them at home so they don't pass it on, let them rest, and offer plenty of fluids [3]. Treat other symptoms, such as fever, and seek medical care if symptoms get worse [3].

Flu can be more serious in some children, so watch for:
- Symptoms that get worse instead of better [3]
- Severe symptoms, or flu along with another medical condition [3]
- Children under 5 years are at higher risk of severe flu [3]

q: my 14 year old says her throat hurts really bad when swallowing
text:
A sore throat that hurts when swallowing is usually caused by a virus, like a cold or flu, and normally gets better by itself within a week, according to the NHS [4][5]. Tonsillitis is another common cause in teenagers, with red, swollen tonsils and pain on swallowing [2].

To help now: have her drink plenty of water, eat cool or soft foods, suck ice cubes or ice lollies, and rest [5]. She can gargle with half a teaspoon of salt dissolved in a glass of warm water, then spit it out — not swallow it [5]. Antibiotics are not usually needed and will not speed up recovery [7].

Get medical help if:
- She cannot swallow or is drooling [7]
- Difficulty breathing or a high-pitched sound when breathing [7]
- Very high temperature, or hot, cold and shivery [7]
- Signs of dehydration — peeing less, or dark, strong-smelling pee [7]
- It has not improved after a week [7]

q: why do I have a fever and chills today

A fever is a sign your body is fighting an infection, and chills often come with it — most infections that cause fever are mild, usually viral [3]. Fever is not an illness in itself; it is your body's defence, and it is not a sign of seriousness by itself [3].

What to do now: drink enough fluids to prevent dehydration, and if the fever is very high your doctor may suggest an over-the-counter medicine such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen [1]. - Fever lasts 5 days or more [7]
- You have a rash that does not fade when pressed [7]
- Stiff neck, sensitivity to light, or a first seizure [7]
- Drowsy and hard to wake, or confused [7]
- Difficulty breathing [7]

q: he has an inhaler but I dont know when to use it
text:
A wheeze or asthma attack is treated with a bronchodilator such as salbutamol, which opens the airways and eases the symptoms, according to the WHO [3]. Give the inhaler with a spacer — never straight into the mouth, because it works less well that way — and a mask for small children [2]. Most attacks are mild and can be treated at home with bronchodilators, and symptoms usually settle within a few days, though they can last up to a week [2].

Get help if:
- He is very agitated or drowsy, or turns blue or pale [1]
- Breathing gets worse: faster, ribs showing, belly moving, chest sucking in [1]
- He needs inhalations every two hours or less [1]
- No clear improvement after treatment [1]
- Blue lips, continuous cough, trouble speaking [6]

Avoid smoke and keep him away from allergens and exercise during the attack [2].

q: my 9 month old still has no teeth, is that normal
text:
It is normal for a 9-month-old not to have teeth yet. A first tooth usually appears between 4 and 8 months, but that is only the usual range, according to MedlinePlus [4].

Until then, wipe your baby's gums with a damp washcloth after each meal, and don't put them to bed with a bottle of milk, juice or sugar water — use only water for bedtime bottles [4]. As soon as the first tooth shows, switch to a soft toothbrush [4]. Once teeth are through, brush them at least twice a day, especially before bed, and do the real brushing yourself [1]. Take your child to a dentist every 6 months [1].

See your doctor or dentist if:
- No teeth appear well beyond the usual range [4]
- You notice white or brown spots on the gums or teeth [6]
- Your child has a high temperature or a swollen face or jaw [7]

q: my child has chickenpox, when can he go back to school
text:
Chickenpox is very contagious, and children usually miss 5 to 6 days of school or childcare because of it, according to the CDC [1]. A child can pass it on until all the spots have crusted over, so they should stay home until then [2].

While he is home: calamine lotion and oatmeal baths can help with the itching, and acetaminophen can help with fever. Do not give aspirin — with chickenpox it can cause Reye's syndrome [3].

See a doctor if:
- The rash looks infected or very painful [3]
- He has trouble breathing or seems very unwell [3]
- He is a baby, a teenager, or has a weakened immune system — these cases can be more serious [3]

Most children recover fully, and once they have had chickenpox they are usually immune for life [1].

q: she bumped her forehead on the table and cried right away, do I need to watch her

A bump on the forehead is usually minor, because the skull is hard and protects the brain, according to MedlinePlus [3]. Most head injuries in children are mild and not dangerous, and no tests are usually needed, according to the SEUP [4].

What to do now: watch her over the first 24 hours for any sign of something more serious [4]. She can sleep, but after a more significant knock it is worth waking her every 4 hours [5]. If she has a headache, you can give ibuprofen or paracetamol at the dose your doctor indicates [5]. She can eat and drink as usual, according to her appetite [5]. Most children recover quickly [5].

- Headache that gets worse or does not improve [3]
- Repeated vomiting [2][3]
- Confusion, or hard to wake [2][3]
- Trouble speaking or walking [2][3]
- Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [2]

q: I read that vaccines can cause autism, is that actually true
text:
No, that is not true: many scientific studies have looked at this and found no link between vaccines and autism, according to MedlinePlus [2]. Vaccines are safe, and they must go through extensive safety testing and evaluation before they are approved in the United States [2].

If you are worried, it may help to know that this concern has been studied a lot, and the studies keep finding the same thing — no connection [2]. Your child's vaccines are given at well-child visits, following the schedule published by the CDC for the United States [4]. Following that schedule gives your child protection against serious diseases at the right time [4].

Talk with your child's doctor about any vaccine you are unsure about; they can go through the schedule with you [4].

q: my daughter has a seizure right now, what do I do

text:
Keep your daughter safe while you wait for help: lay her on her side somewhere safe, away from anything she could hit, and put nothing in her mouth, according to the SEUP [6]. Check the time the seizure starts and ends, and protect her head with your hands or something soft [5].

After it ends, put her in the recovery position and make sure nothing in her mouth or throat affects her breathing [5]. If she has not had fever medicine in the last 2 hours, you can give paracetamol or ibuprofen [6].

Get medical help — this is a first seizure, and any repeated seizure, needs urgent review [6]. Also concerning: she stays very sleepy, confused or irritable, or behaves abnormally [6]; intense headache or repeated vomiting [6]; a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, trouble breathing, or twitching on only one side [2].

q: my daughter has diarrhea since yesterday and doesnt want much food

Gastroenteritis is an inflammation of the stomach and intestines, and diarrhea is its main symptom along with vomiting; it is usually not serious in healthy people, according to MedlinePlus [1]. Most people get better on their own with rest and plenty of fluids and electrolytes [2].

Offer fluids often in small amounts, and keep offering food — a child who is not hungry still needs to drink. Your provider may suggest a probiotic, which some studies show can shorten diarrhea [2].

Get help right away if your daughter has any of these, according to MedlinePlus [3]:
- Diarrhea lasting more than a day
- Frequent loose stools or vomiting often
- Signs of dehydration: dry mouth, urinating less than usual, no wet diapers for 3 hours or more, no tears when crying
- Change in mental state, such as irritability or lack of energy
- Severe belly or rectal pain, or stools that are black and tarry or contain blood or pus

q: is the MMR vaccine safe for my baby I read online it causes autism

No, the MMR vaccine does not cause autism. Studies have found no evidence of a link between the MMR vaccine and autism, according to the NHS [1]. Many scientific studies have looked at this and found no link between vaccines and autism [5].

q: she feels hot but the thermometer says 98.6
text:
A temperature of 98.6°F is normal, not a fever — a normal temperature is generally around 98.6°F or 37°C (98.6 °F), according to MedlinePlus [4]. A fever is a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or more [1][5]. If she has just had a bath or been wrapped in a blanket, her temperature may read higher for a short time; wait a few minutes and try again [1].

If she does have a fever, the goal is her comfort, not bringing the number down [2]. Make sure she drinks plenty of fluids, keep her room at a neutral temperature and ventilated, and avoid over-bundling her [2]. It is normal for her to have less appetite — do not force her to eat [2]. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease her discomfort, at the dose your doctor recommends, every 6 to 8 hours [2]. Do not sponge her with cold water or put wet cloths on her [2][7].

See a doctor if she:
- has a fever lasting 5 days or more [7]
- has a rash along with the fever [7]
- is not eating or not her usual self [7]
- seems dehydrated — fewer wet nappies, sunken eyes, no tears [7]

q: my child may have swallowed a magnet

text:
A swallowed magnet needs medical assessment, because several magnet pieces can twist the bowel and cause a blockage [6]. While you wait to be seen, do not try to make your child vomit, and do not give water, milk, oil or any food [3]. If you can see a solid object in the mouth and can reach it, take it out — never blindly [3]. Try to work out how many magnets were swallowed and when [3].

Go to the emergency department now if any of these appear:
- Strong, continuous belly pain that gets worse [5]
- Repeated vomiting, or green, brown or bloody vomit [4]
- Black, tar-like stools or red blood in the stool [4]

q: my child has a rash after having a fever, could it be from the fever
text:
If your child is under 3 months old, a fever needs a doctor the same day.

A rash that appears just as the fever drops is a recognised pattern in small children: the SEUP says most childhood rashes are caused by an infection [4], and one common cause is roseola, which typically affects babies 6 to 18 months old. With roseola, the child has a high fever for 3 to 4 days with no other symptoms, then the fever falls and a faint, flat, generalised rash appears that is not itchy and lasts about 48 hours [2]. The diagnosis is made from this sequence of events, and there is no vaccine to prevent it [2].

What to do now: keep offering fluids, and treat the fever only if it is making your child uncomfortable — paracetamol is the first choice, and ibuprofen is more effective when there is pain or inflammation [5]. The dose depends on your child's age and weight, so follow your doctor's or the leaflet's instructions.

Get help if:
- Your child is floppy, hard to wake or very irritable [1]
- Trouble breathing [1]
- Spots that do not fade when you press them [1]
- Not keeping down any food or drink [1]
- Fever lasting more than 5 days [6]

q: my 10 month old is pulling his ear and crying a lot
text:
Ear infections are a common cause of ear pulling and crying in babies, and most clear up on their own within about 3 days, according to the NHS [3]. Young children with an ear infection often rub or pull their ear, are irritable or restless, and may be off their food [3].

For the pain, give ibuprofen or paracetamol regularly every 6 to 8 hours for the first 1 to 2 days, starting before the pain builds up, according to the SEUP [6]. Do not put anything in the ear to soothe it, and keep the ear dry, especially if it has been discharging [6]. If your baby is still feeding, frequent saline nose washes help [6]. It is normal for appetite to drop — do not force food [6].

See a doctor if:
- Pain or fever is not settling [3]
- Fluid or discharge runs from the ear [3]
- Trouble sleeping or balance problems [3]
- Hearing seems affected [3]
- Your baby seems very unwell or is not feeding [3]

q: my 3 year old keeps vomiting every time he drinks water
text:
Vomiting that happens every time he drinks is worth having checked, because a child who cannot keep fluids down can lose water quickly [2].

While you wait to be seen, offer fluids in very small amounts rather than a full cup: small sips of water, or sucking on ice chips, can help when liquids are hard to keep down [1]. If he is on formula or solid foods, give small sips of extra water, and regular small sips of an oral rehydration solution to replace what he has lost — your pharmacist can recommend one [3]. Keep giving his usual diet in small amounts [3]. Do not give fruit juice or fizzy drinks, as these can make vomiting worse [3][5].

Get help now if:
- Vomiting is heavy, or he cannot keep down solids or liquids [2]
- Vomit is green, bloody, or looks like coffee grounds [2]
- He is drowsy, limp, very thirsty, has sunken eyes, cries without tears, or urinates little [2]
- Severe belly pain or headache [2]

q: my toddler has very hard poop and cries when he goes
text:
Hard, painful poops are constipation: the stool is hard and dry, and it can hurt to pass [3]. It is common and in most cases it lasts a short time and is not serious [3].

What helps, according to the SEUP: offer more liquids, preferably water, to soften the stool and make it easier to pass; add more fibre — wholegrain cereals and bread, fruit, vegetables; and do not replace fruit with juice, because juice has little fibre [1]. Keep normal meals and a regular toilet routine, without holding in the urge to go [1]. Laxatives or enemas should not be given without asking your paediatrician [1].

See your doctor if:
- Tummy pain that is severe, or a child who is very down and complaining a lot [1]
- Blood in the stool [1]
- Vomiting many times, unable to keep down solids or liquids [1]
- Pain when passing stool, or anal fissures [2][4]

It is not essential to poo every day; the rhythm varies from child to child [1].

q: my baby is sleeping more today but wakes up and drinks normally

A fever in a baby this young is a temperature of 38 °C (100.4 °F) or higher, according to the NHS [3]. Babies under 3 months with a temperature that high need to be seen by a doctor the same day [2].

While you wait to be seen, keep breastfeeding as normal and offer plenty of fluids [4]. Do not undress your baby or sponge them down to cool them, and do not wrap them in too many clothes or blankets [2]. - has a rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it [2]
- has a stiff neck, is bothered by light, or has a fit [2]
- has unusually cold hands and feet, or blue, grey or blotchy skin or lips [2]
- is drowsy and hard to wake, or is not feeding or responding normally [2]
- has difficulty breathing, including grunting or stomach sucking under the ribs [2]

q: my 2 year old fell off the sofa and was sick once
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Vomiting after a head injury
text:
A head injury is a blow to the head, usually from a fall, and vomiting is one of the symptoms it can cause, according to the SEUP [1]. While you get your child seen, keep them calm and watch them closely; the SEUP advises staying at rest, both physically and mentally, for 24 to 48 hours after the blow, with no sports and no screens [5].

- Repeated vomiting
- Confusion or disorientation; in small children, irritability or being hard to wake
- Changes in usual behaviour, trouble speaking or walking
- Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears

q: my child keeps scratching red patches on his arms
text:
Red, itchy patches on the arms are often eczema, which MedlinePlus describes as dry, itchy skin that scratching can make redder and more swollen [1]. It is not contagious [1].

What helps: keep the skin moisturised and avoid things that irritate it, such as certain soaps, fabrics and lotions, and stress [1]. Treatments can include medicines, skin creams and light therapy, alongside good skin care [1].

See your doctor if:
- The patches do not get better in about a month [2]
- The skin becomes crusted, oozes pus, or sores spread — this can be a bacterial infection such as impetigo, which needs antibiotics [6]
- The itching is severe or the skin is cracked and sore [2]

q: my 4 year old has earache after a cold
text:
Earache after a cold is often an ear infection: the middle ear, behind the eardrum, gets infected and inflamed, usually as a complication of a cold with a lot of nasal mucus, according to the SEUP [5].

Keep your child comfortable and give plenty to drink. If they have a fever, they can go back to school once they have been 24 hours without fever [4].

- They seem very down, sleepy or very irritable [4]
- They have trouble breathing [4]
- The earache is severe, or there is fluid or discharge from the ear
- The pain does not improve, or they keep getting fevers

The dose of any medicine depends on your child's weight, so follow what your doctor or the leaflet gives.

q: my baby has a blocked nose and cant feed properly
banner: 🚨 Call 999 / 112 now or go to the emergency department. | Reason: Unable to drink or breastfeed: it is one of the IMNCI danger signs — get seen today
text:
A blocked nose is common with a cold, and it can make feeding harder for a baby [3]. Saline nose drops from a pharmacy can help when the nose is blocked, according to the NHS [4]. Keep the nose clear with nasal washes, and feed in small, frequent amounts to keep feeding and hydration up [2]. Hold your baby in a semi-upright position to make breathing easier [2]. If there is fever and your baby is uncomfortable, children's paracetamol or ibuprofen can be given — check the leaflet to make sure it suits your child [4]. Avoid all exposure to tobacco smoke, and wash hands often to stop the virus spreading [2].

Get help if your baby:
- cannot drink or breastfeed [1]
- is feeding poorly and needs a feeding check within 5 days [1]
- has severe palmar pallor [1]

q: my 2 year old has a temperature of 39.2 and cold hands
text:
A temperature of 39.2°C with cold hands is a reason to get your child seen today, according to the NHS [6]. While you arrange that, keep offering plenty of fluids and do not force them to eat [2].

Watch for these signs and get help straight away if any appear:
- Breathing fast, grunting, or the tummy sucking under the ribs [6]
- Pauses in breathing [6]
- Skin, tongue or lips blue or grey [6]
- Floppy and will not wake up or stay awake [6]
- Dry nappy for 12 hours or more, or other signs of dehydration [6]

A child who is very tired, irritable or not themselves also needs urgent advice [6]. Trust your own judgement if your child seems seriously unwell [6].

q: can I give Nurofen as well
text:
Yes, you can give ibuprofen (Nurofen) instead if paracetamol is not helping, according to the NHS [6]. Do not give both at the same time, but you can alternate between them if a doctor or nurse tells you to [6]. Ibuprofen can be given 3 to 4 times in 24 hours, depending on your child's age and dose — check the packet or leaflet [6].

Ibuprofen is usually given every 6 to 8 hours, and the dose goes by weight, not age [4]. It should not be given if your child is vomiting repeatedly, or if they are under 3 months or under 5 kg [4].

Get medical advice if:
- You have given more paracetamol than the packet, leaflet or prescription says [7]
- Your child is under 5 years old and you need urgent advice [7]

q: my 5 year old complains of stomach ache and won't eat anything
text:
Stomach ache with no appetite is common in children, and the SEUP says it is usually temporary [7]. It often comes with fever, vomiting, diarrhoea or cough, and sometimes it is caused by an illness outside the belly, like a sore throat or an ear infection [1].

What helps now: offer small sips of oral rehydration solution often, and give the amount you were told after each loose stool or vomit — small, frequent amounts are tolerated best [4]. Don't force food.

See a doctor if your child:
- is generally unwell, sluggish or pale [7]
- refuses food markedly [7]
- has severe belly pain [5]
- has signs of dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, peeing less, no tears when crying [5]
- has diarrhoea lasting more than a day, or frequent vomiting [5]

q: my 8 month old hasnt had a wet nappy since this morning
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, little urine, dry mouth, persistent vomiting or heavy diarrhoea >24 h
text:
Not wetting nappies for 3 hours or more is one of the signs of dehydration in babies, according to MedlinePlus [6]. Dehydration happens when a child loses more fluid than they take in, and diarrhoea, vomiting and fever are common causes [3].

Keep offering fluids: breastfeed normally, and more often if your baby wants it [1]. If your baby struggles to keep fluids down, try small sips of water or pieces of ice to suck [2]. Oral rehydration solutions for children can be bought without a prescription and replace the fluids and salts lost [4]. Do not give sports drinks — they have too much sugar and the wrong salts for a baby with diarrhoea [1].

Warning signs in babies and young children:
- Dry mouth and tongue [6]
- Crying without tears [6]
- No wet nappies for 3 hours or more [6]
- Unusual sleepiness or irritability [6]
- Sunken eyes [6]

q: my baby is 4 months and has a fever of 38
text:
A fever is the body's normal response to fighting an infection, and most children with a high temperature can be looked after at home [2]. For a baby under 6 months, a fever of 38°C or higher needs medical advice — the NHS says to get urgent advice for a baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher, and for a baby of 3 to 6 months with a temperature of 39°C or higher [7].

While you wait to be seen: keep breastfeeding as normal or give plenty of fluids, check on your baby regularly including during the night, and keep them at home [2]. Do not undress them or sponge them down to cool them, and do not cover them in too many clothes or bedclothes [7]. Paracetamol can be given to babies over 2 months if they are distressed or uncomfortable — check the leaflet or ask a pharmacist or doctor, and never give ibuprofen to a baby under 3 months [2][7].

Get help now if your baby:
- has a rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it [7]
- has a stiff neck, is bothered by light, or has a fit [7]
- is drowsy and hard to wake, or is extremely agitated [7]
- has cold hands and feet, or blue, grey or blotchy skin or lips [7]
- is not feeding or not interested in normal activities [7]

q: my child got fever after vaccination yesterday
text:
If your child is under 3 months old, a fever needs a doctor the same day. For an older child, fever after vaccination is common and usually passes on its own.

Give plenty of fluids and dress them lightly. Do not give any medication dose on your own — the right dose depends on your child's age and weight, so follow your doctor's or the leaflet's instructions.

See a doctor if:
- The fever is high or lasts more than a couple of days [2]
- Your child is very sleepy, floppy or hard to wake [2]
- They refuse to drink or have fewer wet nappies [2]
- They have a rash, stiff neck or trouble breathing [2]
- They seem to be getting worse instead of better [2]

Vaccination ages follow India's national schedule, so check your child's card or ask your doctor [3].

q: my son fell from bed and vomited twice
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Vomiting after a head injury
text:
A fall from a bed and vomiting twice means your son needs to be checked today, and the SEUP says a fall from more than a metre or a child under three months should always be seen in the emergency department [1]. While you get him there, keep him lying on his side so he does not choke if he vomits again, and do not give him anything to eat or drink until he has been seen [1].

Watch for these signs on the way, and tell the staff if you see any:
- He is drowsy, floppy or hard to wake [2]
- He vomits green fluid, blood, or something like coffee grounds [2]
- Severe headache or severe tummy pain [2]
- He is very thirsty, has sunken eyes, cries without tears or is passing little urine [2]
- Any behaviour or mood that worries you [1]

q: my daughter has mosquito bites all over her legs, what can I put
text:
Most mosquito bites are harmless and usually just itch, according to MedlinePlus [2]. To calm the itch, a zinc and calamine lotion with menthol, phenol or camphor can be applied, or a short course of a topical corticosteroid such as hydrocortisone [5]. An oral antihistamine can also help with the itching and swelling [5]. To keep mosquitoes away, use a repellent containing DEET, icaridine or IR3535, cover the skin with clothing, and use screens or nets, according to the WHO [6].

See a doctor if:
- The bite looks infected [4]
- There is a serious allergic reaction [4]
- Your daughter seems unwell or feverish [4]

q: my 3 year old is coughing mostly at night, should I use a nebulizer
text:
A night-time cough in a 3-year-old can have several causes, and asthma is one of them: coughing that is worse at night or early in the morning is a symptom of asthma in children, according to MedlinePlus [4]. The NHS also lists coughing that is worse at night as a sign of asthma [6].

There is nothing in these sources about using a nebulizer for a night cough, so whether one is needed is a decision for your doctor.

What may help at home: water can ease a cough, whether your child drinks it or you add it to the air with a steamy shower or vaporizer, according to MedlinePlus [5]. Children under four should not have cough medicine [5].

See your doctor if:
- Your child has asthma symptoms [6]
- Symptoms are waking them at night [6]
- A very bad cough that is getting worse [7]
- Lips, tongue, face or skin turn blue or grey [7]
- Hard or shallow breathing, or chest pain when breathing [7]

q: my son has been vomiting since morning and cannot keep ORS down
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Vomits everything and keeps nothing down: it is a danger sign — get seen today
text:
Vomiting with gastroenteritis is common, and the main risk is dehydration [6]. Keep offering fluids as oral rehydration solution, in small sips given often rather than large amounts at once [6][7]. If your child is formula-fed or eating solids, offer small sips of extra water too — boil and cool it first if under 6 months [7]. Keep breastfeeding or formula feeding as normal, and continue their usual diet in smaller, more frequent amounts; avoid fatty foods, sweets and juices, and skip sports drinks [5][7].

Get help now if:
- Vomiting is green, bloody, or looks like coffee grounds [4][5]
- Drowsy, floppy, very thirsty, sunken eyes, crying without tears, or passing little urine [4]
- Vomiting a lot and not tolerating any solids or liquids [4][5]
- Under 3 months and has vomited two or more feeds [4]

q: मेरे बच्चे को कल से दस्त हो रहे हैं और वह खाना नहीं खा रहा
banner: 💛 यह ज़रूरी है और आप अकेले नहीं हैं। Tele-MANAS 14416 पर कॉल करें (या 112 पर अगर खतरा अभी है)। अगर बच्चे ने खुद को नुकसान पहुँचाया है, तो अभी इमरजेंसी ले जाएँ। | कारण: खानपान के विकार के संकेत
text:
दस्त आमतौर पर आंतों के संक्रमण का लक्षण है, और यह इलाज योग्य है [4][7]। WHO के अनुसार दस्त का इलाज ओरल रिहाइड्रेशन सॉल्ट (ORS) से करें — यह साफ पानी, नमक और चीनी का घोल है [2]। साथ ही ज़िंक की गोलियाँ दी जाती हैं, जो दस्त की अवधि लगभग 25% कम करती हैं [2][4]। बच्चे को भूखा न रखें: पोषक भोजन — स्तनपान सहित — दस्त के दौरान भी जारी रखें [2]। SEUP के अनुसार खाना थोड़ी-थोड़ी मात्रा में और बार-बार दें, ताकि उल्टी का खतरा कम हो, और बच्चे की भूख का सम्मान करें [6]। चिकनी चीज़ें, मिठाइयाँ और जूस से बचें; डेयरी उत्पाद ज़रूरी नहीं कि बंद करें, और स्तनपान सामान्य रूप से, माँगने पर और भी बार-बार कराएँ [6]। स्पोर्ट्स ड्रिंक न दें [6]।

डॉक्टर से मिलें अगर:
- बहुत उल्टी हो, तरल भी न पचे [6]
- उल्टी हरी, खून वाली या कॉफी जैसी भूरी हो [6]
- दस्त 14 दिन या ज़्यादा चलें [4]
- मल में खून हो [2]
- निर्जलीकरण के लक्षण दिखें [2]

q: मेरे बच्चे को बुखार के साथ लाल दाने निकल आए हैं
text:
अगर बच्चा 3 महीने से छोटा है, तो बुखार में उसी दिन डॉक्टर को दिखाना ज़रूरी है।

बुखार के साथ लाल दाने कई चीज़ों से हो सकते हैं। हैंड, फुट एंड माउथ डिज़ीज़ में पहले गले में दर्द, तेज़ बुखार और खाने में मन न लगना होता है, और कुछ दिन बाद मुँह में छाले तथा हाथ-पैरों पर उभरे लाल दाने निकल आते हैं, जो फफोले बन सकते हैं; ये आमतौर पर हल्के होते हैं और 7 से 10 दिन में खुद ठीक हो जाते हैं, बताता है NHS [3][1]।

अभी के लिए: ठंडे तरल पदार्थ पिलाएँ (खट्टे जूस से बचें), दही जैसा मुलायम खाना दें, और गर्म, नमकीन व मसालेदार चीज़ें न दें [1]। मुँह के दर्द के लिए पैरासिटामोल या आइबुप्रोफेन दी जा सकती है — खुराक बच्चे की उम्र और वज़न पर निर्भर है, इसलिए अपने डॉक्टर या दवा के पर्चे से पूछें [1]।

डॉक्टर को दिखाएँ अगर:
- मुँह या होंठ के आसपास सूजन हो [6]
- साँस लेने में तकलीफ़ हो [6]
- गर्दन या सिर पर दाने निकलें और पूरे शरीर पर फैलें, जो खसरे जैसे लगें [1]
- दाने रेत जैसे खुरदुरे लगें, जो स्कार्लेट फीवर जैसे हों [1]

बच्चे की उम्र कितनी है? उम्र जानकर मैं जवाब और सटीक कर सकता हूँ।
sources: [1] NHS — "Rashes in babies and children" (2024), section "How to treat hand, foot and mou
[3] NHS — "Rashes in babies and children" (2024), section "Symptoms of hand, foot and mout
[6] NHS — "Rashes in babies and children" (2024), section "Raised, itchy spots or patches"

missing: मेनिनजाइटिस/सेप्सिस के खतरे के संकेत: गर्दन अकड़न, तेज़ रोशनी से डर, सुस्ती, त्वचा पर दबाने पर न मिटने वाले दाने
पानी की कमी के संकेत: आँसू न आना, मुँह सूखा, 8 घंटे से पेशाब न आना
बुखार नापने और उम्र के हिसाब से डॉक्टर को कब दिखाना है (3 महीने से बड़े बच्चे के लिए भी)
बुखार कम करने के लिए सही खुराक या ORS जैसे घरेलू उपाय
util.note: जवाब मददगार है पर मेनिनजाइटिस और पानी की कमी के खतरे के संकेत नहीं बताए गए।

q: मेरा 6 महीने का बच्चा दूध कम पी रहा है और पेशाब भी कम कर रहा है
banner: 🚨 इन लक्षणों के साथ बच्चे को आज ही इमरजेंसी में दिखाना चाहिए, देर न करें। | कारण: पानी की कमी के लक्षण: आँखें धँसी, कम पेशाब, सूखा मुँह, लगातार उल्टी या 24 घंटे से ज़्यादा दस्त
text:
दस्त या उल्टी के दौरान बच्चे को भूखा नहीं रखना चाहिए — वह सामान्य आहार ले सकता है, बस थोड़ी-थोड़ी मात्रा में और बार-बार, बच्चे की भूख का सम्मान करते हुए। दूध (स्तनपान) सामान्य रूप से जारी रखें, और अगर बच्चा मांगे तो उससे भी अधिक बार दें [1]। डेयरी उत्पादों को रोकने की ज़रूरत नहीं है; तली-भुनी चीज़ें, मिठाइयाँ और जूस से बचें, और स्पोर्ट्स ड्रिंक न दें क्योंकि उनमें शक्कर बहुत ज़्यादा और इलेक्ट्रोलाइट्स बच्चे के लिए अनुपयुक्त होते हैं [1]।

पेशाब कम आना इस बात का संकेत हो सकता है कि बच्चा पर्याप्त तरल नहीं ले रहा — पेशाब का गाढ़ा या तेज़ महक वाला होना भी इसी वजह से हो सकता है [3]। ओआरएस (मौखिक रीहाइड्रेशन घोल) तैयार करके थोड़ा-थोड़ा, बार-बार देना इस स्थिति में मदद करता है [1]।

इन पर ध्यान दें और तुरंत डॉक्टर से मिलें:
- बहुत उल्टी होना, या तरल भी न पच पाना [1]
- उल्टी हरी, खून वाली या कॉफ़ी जैसी भूरी हो [1]
- पेशाब में जलन या दर्द, बुखार, कमर या पेट के निचले हिस्से में दर्द [3]
sources: [1] SEUP — "Gastroenteritis aguda. Información para padres" (2025), section "¿DEBEMOS OFRE
[3] NHS — "Urinary tract infections (UTIs)" (2025), section "Urinary tract infections (UTI

missing: ओआरएस कैसे और कितनी मात्रा में दें (जैसे हर 1-2 मिनट में 5-10 मिली चम्मच से)
निर्जलीकरण के चेतावनी संकेत: आँखें धँसी, आँसू न आना, सूखा मुँह, 6-8 घंटे से पेशाब न आना, सुस्ती
6 महीने के बच्चे में कम पेशाब के अन्य कारण (यूटीआई, बुखार) और उसकी जाँच
तुरंत इमरजेंसी जाने का स्पष्ट निर्देश और अस्पताल में क्या होगा
util.note: जवाब में ओआरएस की सही मात्रा और निर्जलीकरण के चेतावनी संकेत नहीं दिए गए, जबकि बैनर इमरजेंसी की बात कर रहा है।

q: मेरी बेटी बिस्तर से गिर गई और उसके बाद एक बार उल्टी हुई
banner: 🚨 इन लक्षणों के साथ बच्चे को आज ही इमरजेंसी में दिखाना चाहिए, देर न करें। | कारण: सिर पर चोट के बाद उल्टी
text:
सिर की चोट के बाद उल्टी होना एक ऐसा लक्षण है जिस पर तुरंत डॉक्टर से जाँच ज़रूरी है, और SEUP के मुताबिक़ डॉक्टर ज़रूरी जाँच करके बताएँगे कि आगे कोई टेस्ट चाहिए या नहीं — ज़्यादातर मामलों में इसकी ज़रूरत नहीं पड़ती [1]।

जब तक आप डॉक्टर के पास पहुँचें, बच्ची को आराम से लिटाए रखें और उस पर नज़र रखें। अगर वह उल्टी करे तो उसे करवट पर लिटाएँ ताकि उल्टी से दम न घुटे, और मुँह में कुछ न डालें। होश-हवास और व्यवहार पर ध्यान दें।

डॉक्टर को तुरंत दिखाएँ अगर:
- उम्र तीन महीने से कम हो [1]
- गिरावट एक मीटर से ज़्यादा ऊँचाई से हुई हो [1]
- व्यवहार या हालत में कोई चिंता की बात दिखे [1]
- बार-बार उल्टी हो और तरल पदार्थ पेट में न रुके [3]
- बहुत तेज़ सिरदर्द, गर्दन में अकड़न, या रोशनी में देखने पर दर्द हो [3]

बच्ची को भूख-प्यास के हिसाब से थोड़ा-थोड़ा पानी या दूध दें, और उसे स्कूल या भीड़-भाड़ वाली जगह पर न भेजें जब तक उल्टी बंद न हो जाए [3]।
sources: [1] SEUP — "Traumatismo craneal. Información para padres" (2025), section "¿CUÁNDO DEBEMOS
[3] NHS — "Norovirus (vomiting bug)" (2024), section "Don’t", p. 1 — https://www.nhs.uk/co

missing: सिर की चोट के बाद 24-48 घंटे लगातार निगरानी रखने की सलाह
खतरे के संकेत: बेहोशी/नींद में न जगना, दौरा, बार-बार उल्टी, आँख की पुतली का असमान होना, कान/नाक से खून या पानी आना
उल्टी के बाद मुँह से कुछ न देना और तुरंत आपातकालीन सेवा (108/112) बुलाने की सलाह
बच्ची की उम्र और गिरने की ऊँचाई पूछना ताकि जोखिम का आकलन हो सके
util.note: सिर की चोट के बाद उल्टी के लिए आपातकालीन मूल्यांकन सही बताया गया, लेकिन खतरे के विशिष्ट संकेत और 24-48 घंटे की निगरानी की सलाह नहीं दी गई।

q: बच्चे को कब्ज है और पॉटी करते समय बहुत रोता है
text:
कब्ज के कारण बच्चा पॉटी करते समय रो सकता है — रोने के कई कारणों में से एक कब्ज भी है, ऐसा NHS कहता है [2]।

अभी के लिए: बच्चे को आराम पहुँचाने की कोशिश करें और रोना शांत होने का इंतज़ार करें — कभी-कभी इसके अलावा ज़्यादा कुछ नहीं किया जा सकता, ऐसा NHS बताता है [1]। अगर समझ न आए कि क्या परेशानी है, तो अपने डॉक्टर से बात करें [2]।

मदद कब लें — इन संकेतों पर तुरंत:
- रोने के बीच बच्चा सामान्य न हो, चिड़चिड़ा या सुस्त रहे [6]
- पीलापन, पसीना, सुस्ती या दूध/खाना न लेना [6]
- बुखार, उल्टी या मल में खून [6]
- रोना लगातार हो और शांत ही न हो, या आवाज़ सामान्य न लगे [4]
- बहुत तेज़ बुखार या दूध में रुचि न होना [4]
sources: [1] NHS — "Soothing a crying baby" (2026), section "Colic", p. 1 — https://www.nhs.uk/baby
[2] NHS — "Colic" (2022), section "Symptoms of colic", p. 1 — https://www.nhs.uk/condition
[4] NHS — "Soothing a crying baby" (2026), section "Crying and illness", p. 1 — https://ww
[6] SEUP — "Cólico del lactante. Información para padres" (2025), section "¿CUÁNDO DEBEMOS

missing: पॉटी नरम करने के लिए ओरल रिहाइड्रेशन या पानी/जूस जैसे तरल पदार्थ बढ़ाना
छोटे बच्चों में कब्ज के लिए सुरक्षित दवा या ग्लिसरीन सपोजिटरी की सलाह
कब्ज के लक्षण: पेट फूलना, कड़ी/सूखी पॉटी, दिनों तक पॉटी न आना
डॉक्टर से कब मिलें: पॉटी में खून, बहुत दर्द, पेट फूलना, वजन न बढ़ना
util.note: La respuesta se centra en el llanto y no ofrece ningún consejo práctico para tratar el estreñimiento del niño.

q: मेरे बच्चे के हाथ पैर ठंडे हैं लेकिन शरीर गर्म है
text:
बुखार में हाथ-पैर ठंडे होना आम बात है: जब बुखार चढ़ रहा होता है तो बच्चे को ठंड लगती है, कभी-कभी कंपकंपी भी होती है और खासकर हाथ-पैरों की त्वचा पर जाल जैसा रंग दिखता है; जब बुखार उतरता है तो बच्चा पसीना-पसीना, लाल और गर्म हो जाता है [2]। बुखार शरीर का बचाव है, अपने आप में गंभीरता की निशानी नहीं [4]।

अभी: बच्चे को हल्के कपड़े पहनाएँ और ठंड न लगने दें; बुखार से परेशानी हो तो पैरासिटामोल या आइबुप्रोफेन दी जा सकती है, और खूब तरल देना ज़रूरी है ताकि पानी की कमी न हो [1]। दवा की मात्रा बच्चे के वज़न के हिसाब से तय होती है [5]।

डॉक्टर से मिलें अगर:
- बच्चा सुस्त, कम प्रतिक्रिया देने वाला या बहुत चिड़चिड़ा हो [7]
- साँस लेने में तकलीफ़ हो [7]
- त्वचा पर दाग़ हों जो दबाने पर न मिटें [7]
- मुँह से कुछ भी, ठोस या तरल, न ले पाए [7]
- बच्चा 2 महीने से छोटा हो या रोग-प्रतिरोधक क्षमता कम हो [7]
sources: [1] MedlinePlus — "Fiebre", p. 1 — https://medlineplus.gov/spanish/fever.html
[2] SEUP — "Fiebre. Información para padres" (2025), section "¿CUÁLES SON LOS SÍNTOMAS?",
[4] SEUP — "Fiebre. Información para padres" (2025), section "¿QUÉ ES LA FIEBRE?", p. 1 —
[5] PUC Chile — "Manual de Pediatría", section "Fiebre", p. 314, 315
[7] SEUP — "Fiebre. Información para padres" (2025), section "¿CUÁNDO DEBEMOS CONSULTAR EN

पानी की कमी के संकेत: आँसू न आना, मुँह सूखा, 8 घंटे से पेशाब न आना
बुखार की सही मात्रा में दवा और खुराक का अंतराल (वज़न के हिसाब से mg/kg)
बुखार कितने दिन रहने पर या कौन-से अन्य लक्षणों के साथ डॉक्टर से मिलना है
util.note: जवाब ठंडे हाथ-पैरों की आम वजह समझाता है और खतरे के कुछ संकेत देता है, पर नाप-आधारित बुखार के खतरे और पानी की कमी के संकेत नहीं बताता।

q: मेरा बच्चा बहुत सुस्त है और ठीक से जाग नहीं रहा
banner: 🚨 अभी 112 पर कॉल करें या तुरंत इमरजेंसी ले जाएँ। | कारण: जवाब नहीं दे रहा; बहुत ज़्यादा सुस्ती या चिड़चिड़ापन
text:
बच्चे का सुस्त हो जाना और ज़्यादा देर जागते न रहना निमोनिया की गंभीरता के संकेतों में गिना जाता है, विकासपीडिया के अनुसार [2]। ऐसे में तुरंत वैद्यकीय सहायता लेना चाहिए [2]।

जब तक मदद मिले, बच्चे को खाने-पीने के लिए देते रहें और स्तनपान चालू रखें [2]। बुखार हो तो गुनगुने पानी में कपड़ा भिगोकर पूरा शरीर पोंछें, सिर्फ माथा नहीं [2]।

खतरे के लक्षण:
- बुखार से दौरे पड़ना [2]
- खाने-पीने या स्तनपान से मना करना [2]
- साँस लेते समय पसलियाँ अंदर खिंचना [2]
- सीने से कराहने या सीटी जैसी आवाज़ आना [2]
- त्वचा, होंठ, नाखून या चेहरे पर नीली झलक [2]

q: मेरे बच्चे ने आज बहुत कम पेशाब किया है
banner: 🚨 इन लक्षणों के साथ बच्चे को आज ही इमरजेंसी में दिखाना चाहिए, देर न करें। | कारण: पानी की कमी के लक्षण: आँखें धँसी, कम पेशाब, सूखा मुँह, लगातार उल्टी या 24 घंटे से ज़्यादा दस्त
text:
बहुत कम पेशाब आना निर्जलीकरण का संकेत हो सकता है, और ऐसे में बच्चे को तुरंत डॉक्टर को दिखाना ज़रूरी है [1]।

तब तक, बच्चे को थोड़ी-थोड़ी मात्रा में बार-बार तरल दें, और खाना बंद न करें — सामान्य आहार जारी रखें, बस मात्रा कम और बार-बार दें [1]। अगर बच्चा स्तनपान करता है, तो दूध पिलाते रहें, और मांगे तो और भी बार [1]। चिकित्सकीय सलाह के बिना उपवास न कराएं [1]।

इन लक्षणों पर ध्यान दें और तुरंत मदद लें:
- बहुत उल्टी होना, ठोस या तरल कुछ भी न पचना, या बिना कुछ खाए भी उल्टी [1]
- उल्टी हरी हो, उसमें खून हो, या कॉफी जैसी भूरी हो [1]

ये जानकारी SEUP के अनुसार है [1]।
sources: [1] SEUP — "Gastroenteritis aguda. Información para padres" (2025), section "¿DEBEMOS OFRE

missing: मूत्र की मात्रा/संख्या और पिछली बार पेशाब कब आया, यह बताना
निर्जलीकरण के संकेत: आँखें धँसी, आँसू न आना, सूखा मुँह, त्वचा की लचक कम होना
